name: Buteyko breathing

lead: The Buteyko method teaches nasal breathing, reduced breathing and relaxation. It was developed by Ukrainian physiologist Konstantin Buteyko in the Soviet Union in the 1950s, on the theory that chronic over-breathing drives conditions such as asthma.

In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed as a way to encourage nasal breathing, correct mouth breathing and calm anxiety, with the idea that breathing habits support facial development. Research has focused almost entirely on asthma, where small trials suggest possible symptom and quality-of-life benefits with little change in lung function. No studies test it for appearance.

paras: Practitioners aim to breathe less, breathe through the nose and relax, tracking progress with a breath-hold time called the control pause. Some users pair it with mouth taping during sleep. It is taught in sessions and practised daily.

The sources reviewed describe no specific adverse events. Medical commentators object to broad claims, such as reduced medication use, that lack adequate evidence, so people with asthma are advised to keep following their doctor's plan.

chain: Better breathing habits, claimed facial benefit
angle.text: Buteyko is a breathing-retraining method that looksmaxxing users connect with nasal breathing, mouth taping and the idea that breathing habits shape the face. Less mouth breathing is the step people count on for a facial benefit. Trials in asthma show modest symptom effects, and none test facial appearance.

lead: The Buteyko method is a breathing-retraining system built around nasal breathing, deliberately reduced breathing volume and relaxation. It was developed by the Soviet physician Konstantin Buteyko from the 1950s on the theory that chronic over-breathing (hyperventilation) and the resulting low carbon dioxide contribute to conditions such as asthma.[1][2]

People in appearance-focused communities use it as a route to habitual nasal breathing. The chain they describe runs from practicing nasal, reduced breathing to breathing through the nose by day and night, and from there to the oral posture, facial development and calm that they associate with a better looking face; some pair it with mouth taping during sleep.[3] Wikipedia notes that chronic mouth breathing in children may affect dental and facial growth and may contribute to a long, narrow face, while also noting the relationship may run in both directions.[4]

Research on the method has centered almost entirely on asthma, where randomized trials report improvements in symptoms, quality of life and reliever use with little change in lung function.[1][5][6][7][8][9] No published study has tested Buteyko breathing for facial appearance or nasal shape.

paras: The method holds that chronic hyperventilation and hypocapnia (low blood carbon dioxide) contribute to a wide range of illnesses, with proposed effects including airway muscle spasm (bronchospasm) and disturbed cell energy production.[1] Its three core principles are nasal breathing, reduced breathing and relaxation.[1]

Nasal breathing: proponents say the nose humidifies, warms and cleans inhaled air, link mouth breathing and poor posture to poor sleep, and recommend nasal breathing during exercise.[1] Reduced breathing: exercises deliberately lower breathing volume, and teachers compare learning them to learning to ride a bicycle, with the exercises phased out over time.[1] Relaxation: the method aims to stop the initial over-breathing at the start of an asthma attack from escalating into a vicious circle.[1]

Practitioners use the control pause, the time a person can comfortably hold their breath after exhaling, as a measure of progress; teachers say improvement appears as a longer pause and lower pulse rate.[1] Advocates have claimed it can help as many as 150 conditions, including asthma, COPD and diabetes.[1]

Konstantin Buteyko was born in 1923 in Ivanitsa, Ukraine, began studying mechanics at Kyiv Polytechnic Institute, and after wartime service enrolled at the First Moscow Institute of Medicine in 1946, graduating in 1952.[2] As a student he studied links between patients' breathing rates and illness severity; he said he developed his method in 1952 after being diagnosed with malignant hypertension at age 29, reporting that reducing his breathing relieved symptoms.[2] He began a clinical trial of 200 patients in 1959, and his wife Ludmila, who learned of his work from a newspaper in 1969, later became a teacher of the method.[2] His 1990 book was titled The Buteyko Method, An Experience of Use in Medicine, and he died in Moscow on 2 May 2003, aged 80.[2]

A first official study on asthma was conducted in 1968 at the Leningrad Institute of Pulmonology, and after a second study at the First Moscow Institute of Pediatric Diseases the Soviet health ministry issued Order No. 591 in April 1980 providing for its use in bronchial asthma.[1] The method later spread to Australia, New Zealand, Britain and the United States, where accounts of dramatic improvement circulate online and in books and are anecdotal.[1] In 2019 the Indonesian singer Andien posted photos of herself and her family with tape over their mouths, which drew renewed interest.[1]

In English-language forums the method surfaces in breathing, anxiety and strength-training communities: T Nation members have mentioned Buteyko's work on breathing volume and asthma, with one saying he is not totally sold, another saying it has helped many people with allergies, and another describing looking into it after waking unrefreshed as a long-time mouth breather.[10][11][12]

A 1998 blinded randomized trial of 39 adults and adolescents with asthma in Australia compared Buteyko techniques with control classes over three months: the Buteyko group cut daily beta-2 agonist use significantly more and showed lower minute ventilation, while inhaled steroid use and quality of life trended toward benefit and peak flow and FEV1 did not change.[7] A 2000 randomized trial of 36 adults used a Buteyko video versus a placebo video at home for four weeks and reported greater quality-of-life improvement and reduced bronchodilator use.[9]

A 2003 randomized trial of 90 adults on inhaled corticosteroids compared Buteyko, a pranayama-mimicking device and a placebo device for six months; Buteyko improved symptoms and reduced bronchodilator use but did not change bronchial responsiveness, FEV1 or exacerbations.[8] A 2008 randomized trial of Buteyko as an adjunct to conventional management found both Buteyko and a physiotherapist-taught breathing and relaxation control improved similarly at six months, with significantly less inhaled corticosteroid use in the Buteyko group.[5] A 2013 randomized trial of 120 adults compared Buteyko, pranayama and routine medication alone for three months, with Buteyko superior to control for asthma quality of life and not significantly different from pranayama.[13]

A 2020 Cochrane review of breathing exercises for adults with asthma (22 studies, 2,880 participants, mostly yoga or breathing retraining) found improved quality of life and reduced hyperventilation symptoms at three months with moderate-certainty evidence, with certainty for other outcomes ranging from moderate to very low.[6] A 2014 Scottish (SIGN) guideline said the method may improve some symptoms and quality of life but has little effect on lung function, and a 2015 Australian government review of alternative therapies found no clear evidence of effectiveness for Buteyko.[1] Reviewers have noted small samples, inconsistent designs and difficulty with blinding.[1]

A 2008 study of 83 adults examined Buteyko's claim that breath-holding time reflects chronic hyperventilation and found breath-holding time did not predict resting end-tidal carbon dioxide, though shorter breath-holding correlated with a chest-dominant breathing pattern in people with abnormal spirometry.[14] A 2001 BMJ survey of treated adults with asthma at one practice found about 29 percent scored in the range suggesting dysfunctional breathing, and its authors suggested this may partly explain the anecdotal success of the Buteyko method.[15]
No trials were found on the use of Buteyko breathing for facial appearance or nasal shape.

Nasal breathing is one of the three Buteyko principles and the point where the method meets appearance communities.[1] Wikipedia describes chronic mouth breathing as most often an adaptation to nasal congestion, notes that nasal breathing filters and warms air, and says mouth breathing in children may affect dental and facial growth, citing mainly orthodontic textbooks and older sources and noting some effects are hedged or lack citations.[4]

A 2025 systematic review of nighttime mouth taping identified 10 studies with 213 patients; two reported significant improvement in sleep apnea markers, the others found no differences and noted potential risks such as asphyxiation when nasal obstruction is present, and the authors described indiscriminate use as a potentially serious risk of harm.[16] A 2025 scoping review found nine studies and reviewed 50 TikTok videos; its authors reported possible benefits for sleep apnea, snoring and ventilation mask leak in some studies and no benefit in one asthma study, and called for higher-quality research.[16]

On looksmax.org, one thread titled as a Buteyko method post describes it as a free way to reduce anxiety and asthma symptoms, and argues that breathing less raises carbon dioxide and produces calm.[3] A reply links mouth breathing to palate and tonsil changes and says correct nighttime breathing is hard with such changes, and another user reports taping the mouth with micropore tape while sleeping.[3] These are user claims; no published studies tested them.

No specific adverse events of the exercises are described in the trials above. Some members of the medical community have been skeptical because of what Bruton and Thomas called exaggerated and unsubstantiated claims by earlier practitioners, and reviews have questioned whether altering carbon dioxide levels in asthma is desirable or achievable.[1] Wikipedia notes that high-quality trials are scarce and that most research is on asthma with a small amount on sleep apnea.[1] Mouth taping reviews note an asphyxiation risk where nasal obstruction is present.[16]
